abstract: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are major pathophysiological events implicated in various brain diseases. Hallmarks of SD include a negative DC shift, reflecting near-complete neuronal depolarization, and the depression of cortical activity. Using microelectrode field potential recordings from the rat cortex, we found that, in contrast to the depression of activity in conventional AC frequency bands (0.5-1000 Hz), high-potassium-induced SDs were associated with increased local field potential power at ultra-fast frequencies (4-8 kHz), which we term the Ultra-Fast Signal (UFS). UFSs were time-locked to the SD-related DC shifts, although their peaks were delayed relative to those of the DC shifts. Furthermore, UFS magnitude and duration correlated with those of the DC shift, and UFSs exhibited vertical propagation profiles across cortical depth similar to DC shifts. During partial superficial SDs, UFSs were confined to the cortical layers recruited by the SD. UFSs were also prominent in SD clusters during isoelectric SDs, occurring against a background of suppressed AC activity. We propose that the UFS could serve as an additional SD marker that is particularly useful for detecting isoelectric SDs.
